item.title: Was the American 'Cheetah' Really a Cheetah After All?
item.description: Ancient DNA shows the speedy Ice Age cat that once chased North America's pronghorn was actually a puma in disguise.

item.title: Could a $100 Detector Really See Invisible Particles Falling from Space?
item.description: Tiny particles from space pass through our bodies every second, but a pocket-sized detector built from $100 in parts can catch them — and it's now used by students and scientists around the world.

item.title: What Does a Mysterious Wall in Morocco Reveal About Ancient Africa?
item.description: In the hills of north-west Morocco, an old wall overlooking a river turns out to be roughly 4,000 years old — the earliest confirmed defensive construction in North Africa beyond Egypt, and a sign that the region was anything but a backwater.

item.title: How a £30m Public Appeal Saved Rothbury Estate for Wildlife
How Does Saturn's Icy Moon Make Hidden Clues to Life Easier to Find?
item.description: Enceladus sprays bits of its hidden ocean into space. New lab experiments show the frozen droplets separate their salts on the way up, quietly concentrating the clues scientists hope to find.

item.title: Why Did Crocodiles Survive the Asteroid That Killed the Dinosaurs?
item.description: Sixty-six million years ago an asteroid wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs, yet crocodiles and their ancient relatives lived on. New research suggests the secret was simple: they loved warm weather, and the tropics stayed warm enough to shelter them.

item.title: What Do Quark Wakes Teach Us About the Universe's Primordial Soup?
How Did World Countries Agree to Protect 30% of Earth by 2030?
item.description: At the COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia, countries reached a deal to implement the 2022 Global Biodiversity Framework — but the big missing piece is money.

item.title: How Did Scientists Read a 2,000-Year-Old Scroll by Burning a Brand-New One?
item.description: Nearly 2,000 years ago, Mount Vesuvius turned a Roman library into lumps of black charcoal. Now scientists have found a clever trick for peering inside those fragile scrolls — and to test it, they burned some brand-new ones of their own.

item.title: How Did One New Skull Fragment Push Homo erectus Back 200,000 Years?
item.description: A dusty box of fossils from a South African cave sat unstudied for decades. Among them was something no one expected: the oldest adult Homo erectus skull piece ever found.

item.title: Was the early universe really as pristine as scientists thought?
item.description: Astronomers long imagined the young cosmos as a nearly empty place made of hydrogen and helium. New James Webb Space Telescope observations show some early galaxies were already spreading carbon, oxygen, and silicon — the stuff of planets and living things — just 500 million years after the Big Bang.

item.title: What Does Northern Ireland's New Plan to Bring Nature Back Actually Promise?
item.description: Northern Ireland just launched a long-term Nature Recovery Strategy to restore habitats and halt biodiversity loss — here's what it sets out to do, and why it matters far beyond one corner of the map.

item.title: How Did a Spacecraft Use Earth as a Slingshot to Reach Jupiter?
item.description: A European spacecraft on its way to Jupiter just swung past Earth at 8,640 km above the Indian Ocean — borrowing our planet's gravity to speed up without burning precious fuel.

item.title: How Did Thousands of Strangers Buy a Whole English Estate?
item.description: A 9,500-acre slice of English countryside went up for sale for the first time in centuries — so 25,000 ordinary people chipped in to buy it together and hand it back to nature.

item.title: How Did Antarctica's First Dinosaur Bone Hide in a Drawer for 40 Years?
item.description: A small fossil collected on an icy Antarctic island in 1985 sat forgotten in a museum drawer for four decades — until a curious scientist opened it and realised it was the first dinosaur bone ever found on the continent.

item.title: What Makes a Golden Eagle Chick Called Beaky Junior So Important?
item.description: A young golden eagle named Beaky Junior has become the first chick to fledge from a managed grouse moor in southern Scotland — and his flight marks a comeback three centuries in the making.

item.title: How Does Vitamin A Help Build the Sharpest Part of the Human Eye?
item.description: There's a tiny patch at the very centre of your retina that handles about half of everything you see. New research shows how a molecule made from vitamin A helps build it before birth — and overturns a 30-year-old idea about how eyes take shape.

item.title: How Could a Glacier Help Move Stonehenge's Six-Ton Altar Stone?
item.description: The Altar Stone at Stonehenge came from Scotland, 435 miles away — and for years nobody could agree how it got there. A new study suggests an ancient ice sheet may have done the first part of the journey, leaving people to finish the job.

item.title: Did Neanderthals Use Birch Bark Glue as an Ancient Medicine?
item.description: Long before modern antibiotics, our close cousins the Neanderthals may have been dabbing a sticky, home-made balm onto cuts and scrapes. A new study finds that birch tar — the gooey glue they crafted from bark — naturally fights the very bacteria that turn wounds septic.

item.title: Can We Turn Seawater Into Drinking Water Without Leaving Any Waste Behind?
item.description: Engineers at the University of Rochester have built a solar-powered panel that turns ocean water into fresh water — and turns the leftover salt into something useful instead of waste.
